metric: Share of U.S. public high schools offering a foundational CS course
caption: of U.S. public high schools offer a foundational computer science course.
source: Code.org, CSTA & ECEP Alliance, 2025 State of AI + Computer Science Education
notes: Report text: 'Currently, 60% of high schools offer foundational CS courses.' The national trend chart shows 47%, 51%, 53%, 58%, 60%, 60% for 2019-20 through 2024-25, so access was flat between the last two years. The Dec 10, 2025 Code.org release says 'U.S. public high schools'.

metric: Effect on log annual earnings at age 24 of a student's high school starting to offer high-quality CS courses while the student was enrolled
caption: higher earnings at age 24 for Maryland students whose high school started offering high-quality computer science while they were there.
data_year: Maryland public high schools that added high-quality CS courses, 2015 to 2020 (earnings at age 24, in 2021 dollars)
source: Liu, J., Conrad, C., & Blazar, D., Computer Science for All? The Impact of High School Computer Science Courses on College Majors and Earnings (EdWorkingPaper No. 24-904), Annenberg Institute at Brown University, January 2024 version
notes: Paper text (printed p. 4): 'unexpected HQ CS exposure raised students’ likelihood of being employed by 2.6 percentage points and annual earnings by about 8 percent at age 24.' Printed p. 27: 'the positive effects of HQ CS exposure on log earnings at age 24 are primarily concentrated among students who are females, FARMS, Black, and in the top quartile of the mathematics achievement distribution. All of these effects are at least marginally significant and are in the range of 10 to 14 percent.' Table 8 (printed p. 51), reduced-form estimates on log earnings at 24: full sample 0.0802 (p<0.05); Black students 0.1203 (p<0.05, N = 10,449). The +12% is that coefficient rounded; it is a log-point estimate. Caveats: these are reduced-form effects of a high school offering high-quality (HQ) CS courses while the student was enrolled, not of taking one course; the paper says its estimates of taking a course (IV) are imprecise and it focuses on the reduced form. Earnings are conditional on having observed earnings at 24. Code.org's Dec 10, 2025 release describes this as 'A single high school CS course increases future earnings by 8%', which overstates what the paper measured, so the site cites the paper instead.

metric: Low-income students' share of all students vs. share of foundational CS students
caption: Low-income students are 53% of students but 38% of those in foundational computer science.
source: Alyson Klein, "One Change That Can Get More Girls, Students of Color Taking Computer Science," Education Week, Oct 22, 2024, citing Code.org's 2024 State of CS report
notes: Article text: 'Students from low-income families comprise 53 percent of students but make up 38 percent of those in foundational computer science courses.' The article says 'students', not 'high school students'. It cites Code.org's annual report and does not give the number of reporting states for this figure.
